name: Lumenac
description: A targeted neuroactive compound that specifically enhances the processing pathways associated with optical and auditory augments, sharpening the brain's ability to interpret augment-transmitted sensory data without increasing raw augment hardware output. The effect is subtle compared to hardware-level boosters — Lumenac doesn't make your eyes see further, it makes your brain process what your eyes already send with greater speed and fidelity. Users describe colors becoming more distinct, audio streams separating into individually identifiable components, and low-light augment feeds resolving with film-like clarity.
effects: Optical augment data processed with 60% greater fidelity and speed
Color discrimination enhanced — subtle gradients become distinct
Auditory augment streams separated and individually processable
Low-light and thermal augment feeds sharpen significantly
Reaction time to visually-detected threats reduced by 25-35ms
side_effects: Photosensitivity in users with high-grade optical augments
Auditory sensory overload in loud environments
Mild visual static on come-down as processing normalizes
Frequent use degrades organic visual cortex integration (the brain becomes reliant on the augment pathway)
Rare: optical augment firmware conflicts causing visual glitching
cultural_context: Lumenac sits in a comfortable gray zone — it's prescription but widely available on the street, and the dose differential between 'clinically useful' and 'street recreational' is small enough that enforcement is inconsistent. Snipers, surveillance operators, and artists with optical augments all use it. There's a small but dedicated subculture of visual artists who use Lumenac to experience their own work differently — the enhanced color discrimination turns ordinary visual art into an overwhelming sensory event. The ocular delivery method (drops directly onto the optical augment's interface membrane) makes it discreet and fast-acting.
story_hooks: A corporate surveillance analyst has been using Lumenac daily for three years and can no longer process visual information through his unaugmented eye — the brain rewiring is so complete that his organic eye now feels like watching the world through frosted glass.

A batch of Lumenac on the street has been laced with a compound that, at peak effect, causes optical augments to record and transmit everything the user sees to an unknown receiver — someone is building a surveillance network through recreational drug users.

A Shelf artist who can't afford proper optical augments has discovered that Lumenac interacts with her basic-grade chrome in a way that produces visual effects no one has documented — she's experiencing colors that don't exist in standard human or augment visual spectra, and Helix researchers are very interested in why.
